A new study now reports the mechanistic link between lipid droplet formation and ferroptosis regulation during infection, centering on a regulatory axis the authors describe as RGS4-HERC2-NCOA4-FTH. According to the study, rabies virus upregulates Regulator of G Protein Signaling 4 (RGS4), a ferroptosis-associated regulator, and this induction depends strictly on triglyceride synthesis and subsequent lipid droplet formation. Functionally, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of RGS4 elevates ferroptosis susceptibility, which in turn restricts viral replication. The mechanistic chain works as follows. When RGS4 is depleted, levels of HERC2 fall, impairing the assembly of branched K48/K63 ubiquitin chains on NCOA4. These chains are essential for NCOA4’s proteasomal degradation, so their loss stabilizes NCOA4. Stabilized NCOA4 then promotes ferritinophagy, the autophagic degradation of ferritin, leading to loss of ferritin heavy chain (FTH) and ultimately inducing ferroptosis. The lyssavirus matrix (M) protein directly counteracts this pathway. The researchers found that M protein inhibits RGS4 degradation via the Cys/N-degron system through incomplete autophagy, thereby stabilizing RGS4. Maintained RGS4 preserves HERC2 expression, promotes NCOA4 ubiquitination, and attenuates ferritinophagy. This reduces ferroptosis susceptibility and enables viral replication. The findings, reported in PLOS Pathogens, unveil what the authors describe as a novel lyssavirus-specific regulatory axis that modulates ferroptosis, highlighting the role of ferroptosis in lyssavirus infection and pathogenesis. The work is based on cell biological and mechanistic experiments described in the study, and the reported pathway links viral protein function to iron metabolism and autophagy during infection. A new study now reports that a gene-silencing approach delivered by a viral vector can sharply suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and substantially improve survival in infected mice, both when administered before infection and when given after the virus has already entered the body. The research, published as a short communication in the journal Animal Diseases, focused on recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2, or rAAV2, as a delivery vehicle for short interfering RNAs, commonly called siRNAs. These small RNA molecules can silence specific genes by binding to their messenger RNA transcripts and triggering their degradation. The team designed siRNAs targeting two rabies virus genes: the G gene, which encodes the glycoprotein responsible for neuronal entry and transport, and the L gene, which encodes the RNA polymerase catalytic subunit essential for viral transcription and replication. The researchers first screened six candidate siRNAs, three against each target gene, in mouse neuroblastoma cells and baby hamster kidney cells infected with the rabies virus CVS-11 strain. Direct immunofluorescence assays showed that four of the candidates, si-G193, si-G672, si-G997, and si-L5055, significantly inhibited viral replication, with a marked reduction in fluorescent spots per field of view. Viral titer measurements confirmed that si-G997 and si-L5055 produced significantly lower titers than the negative control. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR revealed that all siRNAs targeting the G gene effectively reduced G messenger RNA levels in both cell types, while si-L5055 significantly decreased L messenger RNA levels. To verify that these effects reflected true gene knockdown rather than indirect antiviral activity, the team cotransfected human embryonic kidney cells with either si-G997 or si-L5055 together with plasmids expressing tagged rabies virus G or L proteins. Both siRNAs significantly reduced the expression of their respective target proteins compared with a scrambled negative control. Under infection conditions, the protein levels of the viral N and G proteins were reduced by both siRNAs, and the G protein was suppressed more markedly than the N protein. The authors attributed the poor performance of the other four siRNAs to differences in the thermodynamic properties of the target sequences and target site accessibility. Chemically synthesized siRNAs, although rapid in silencing target genes, are prone to degradation in the body and act only briefly. Viral vectors such as adenovirus, retrovirus, and lentivirus can deliver nucleic acids but often provoke strong host immune responses that generate neutralizing antibodies and weaken therapeutic effects. The researchers therefore turned to adeno-associated virus, which they describe as a relatively safe delivery system that supports long-term episomal expression in most tissues. Serotype 2 was chosen because most AAV vectors show predominant tropism for liver and muscle, whereas serotype 2 specifically targets the central nervous system, a property that fits the requirements of rabies virus research. The team encapsulated siRNA expression cassettes, each containing a CMV enhancer, a U6 promoter, and a shRNA coding sequence, into the rAAV2 vector, producing the constructs rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055. In HEK293T cells, these vectors significantly reduced the expression of the G protein and L protein, respectively. A CCK-8 assay showed that neither vector affected the viability of BHK-21 cells. When BHK-21 cells were transduced with the vectors 24 hours before rabies virus infection, both N and G protein levels decreased compared with a negative control vector, with the reduction in G expression more pronounced. In neuroblastoma cells transduced with rAAV-G997, G messenger RNA levels and viral titers remained consistently lower than in the control group at all time points examined, and rAAV-L5055 similarly reduced L messenger RNA levels and viral titers at every time point. The in vivo experiments used six-week-old Kunming mice divided into groups of ten. Three groups received intracerebral injections of rAAV2 at a dose of 2 × 1011 vector genomes per kilogram, followed 48 hours later by an intramuscular challenge with 1 × 105 focus-forming units of the CVS-11 strain. Among mice injected with rAAV-G997, rAAV-L5055, or a negative control vector before infection, the rAAV-G997 group maintained relatively stable body weight throughout a 21-day observation period, while survival rates reached 90 percent for rAAV-G997, 90 percent for rAAV-L5055, and 50 percent for the control. In a postexposure setting, mice received the same vectors 24 hours after viral challenge. The rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055 groups again showed relatively stable body weight changes compared with the control group, and survival rates were 88.9 percent for both treatment groups versus 55.6 percent for the control. A separate confirmatory experiment using 18 additional mice, six per group, measured viral loads in brain tissue on day 7 after infection. Both pretreatment groups exhibited significantly decreased viral loads in brain tissue compared with the negative control. The authors note that the lack of significant difference in efficacy between the two vectors suggests the strategy has a broad therapeutic window. The protective effect is attributed to two factors. Rabies virus primarily infects the central nervous system, and AAV2 exhibits natural tropism for neurons, enabling efficient transduction of the primary sites of viral replication when delivered directly to the brain. Intracerebral injection also bypasses the blood-brain barrier, delivering the therapeutic vector straight to the brain parenchyma. Consequently, even 24 hours after viral challenge, the vector-delivered siRNAs effectively suppressed viral replication within the central nervous system, an intervention that directly targets the intracellular viral life cycle and offers a prolonged therapeutic window that the authors say surpasses that of conventional biologics. The translational path faces considerable hurdles. The evaluations indicated that a relatively high viral dose is required for efficacy, which increases production costs. Owing to time constraints, the study was unable to assess the purity of the packaged rAAV2, and product-related impurities such as empty capsids may cause batch-to-batch variability and potentially exacerbate host immune responses. The authors conclude that rAAV2-mediated delivery of siRNAs targeting the rabies virus G and L genes can inhibit viral replication in vitro and provide significant protection in vivo, highlighting the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies while acknowledging that addressing manufacturing and purity issues remains critical for any future clinical application. County Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis said the second rabid raccoon “is an important reminder to never touch, handle, or feed any wild animals, even when they appear healthy.” He urged residents to keep their distance from wildlife, report sick or unusually behaving animals to local animal control and ensure their pets are up to date on rabies vaccinations. records.content: Open menu NTD Television U.S.ChinaWorldPoliticsHealthBusinessEntertainmentSports More ●LIVE search EN▼ NTD Television Health News US Rabies Surge Prompts Public Health Warning As recently as Oct. 11, the Pasadena Public Health Department in California reported finding an infected bat along East Green Street between South Marengo and South Euclid Avenues. By Juliette Fairley | Published: 10/26/2026, 12:19:29 PM EDT Raccoon. (Unsplash) A surge in animal rabies cases across the U.S. has led federal health officials and professional veterinary organizations to issue public health warnings. From July through August, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) documented 17 percent more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025, including reports of events involving more than one person being exposed. “Several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events have highlighted the importance of performing careful rabies risk assessment,” the CDC said in a statement online. A veterinarian worker network called Vet Candy is calling for domestic pet vaccinations against rabies because infected wildlife, such as bats and raccoons, are a risk to both humans and their furry companions. For example, a cat found near 11th Street NW and Moorman Avenue NW in Roanoke, Virginia, on Oct. 9 tested positive for rabies, according to a Virginia Department of Health statement online. In California, the Pasadena Public Health Department reported finding an infected bat on Oct. 11 along East Green Street between South Marengo and South Euclid Avenues. It is the city's third reported rabid bat of the year. “Although human rabies infections remain rare in the United States, the virus continues to circulate among wildlife, creating opportunities for exposure when infected animals come into contact with people, pets, or other animals,” a Vet Candy alert states. Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that is nearly 100 percent fatal once clinical symptoms emerge in either animals or humans. However, it is preventable with vaccination. About 100,000 Americans receive a rabies vaccination after possible exposure every year, according to the CDC, and the animals most frequently reported infected with rabies are bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes. A pallid bat flying over a pond at night in a file photo. Shutterstock Last month, the CDC issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) health advisory in response to increases in human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals. “One of the biggest misconceptions about rabies is that infected animals always appear aggressive,” Vet Candy authorities said. “While aggression can be a clinical sign, rabid animals may also become unusually friendly, disoriented, weak, or unable to walk normally.” Once infected with a bite or scratch, health care providers can administer post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) to prevent rabies from spreading and causing death. The CDC advises clinicians that it’s important to administer PEP appropriately because errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could result in potential adverse effects and avoidable costs. “For persons who have never been vaccinated against rabies, PEP should always include [human rabies immune globulin] HRIG and vaccine,” CDC authorities said. “Persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies should receive vaccine on days 0 and 3 and should not receive HRIG.”

records.content: NORTH SMITHFIELD, R.I. (WPRI) — The Rhode Island Department of Health is warning residents in Pawtucket and North Smithfield that three raccoons have tested positive for rabies. The Health Department confirmed a rabid raccoon was found near Black Plain Road in North Smithfield this week. Two more rabid raccoons were also discovered in “close proximity to each other” near Wilcox and Blaisdell avenues, according to the Health Department. The two Pawtucket raccoons were found roughly a mile away from where another rabid raccoon was found on Hope Street in Providence last week. While there were no known human exposures to the raccoons in Pawtucket, the Health Department said a dog and two residents are receiving post-exposure treatment in North Smithfield. The Health Department has identified 46 rabid wild animals so far this year. This is nearly two times the annual average of 25 rabid animals reported between 2021 and 2025. Anyone who may have also had direct contact with the raccoons should call the Health Department’s Center for Acute Infectious Disease Epidemiology at 401-222-2577. Rabies is a potentially deadly viral disease that typically spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) . The rabies virus primarily affects the central nervous system and, if left untreated, almost always results in death. The animals most frequently infected with rabies locally are bats, skunks, raccoons and foxes, according to the Health Department. Humans who are exposed to rabies are given a series of shots over four to five weeks to ensure the virus doesn’t spread throughout the body. The CDC notes that, once the rabies virus advances past the incubation period to the onset of symptoms, there is no effective treatment for it. Rhode Island law requires dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies. This not only prevents them from contracting rabies, but also spreading the disease to humans and other pets. Below are some rabies prevention tips from the Health Department: Make sure all dogs, cats and ferrets are up to date on rabies vaccinations. Avoid all contact with and do not feed stray or free-roaming domestic animals. Avoid all contact with and do not feed wild animals. Do not feed your animals outdoors, as this will attract other animals. This is especially dangerous when feeding large numbers of free-roaming cats. Protect your pets by always maintaining control; walk dogs on a leash or let them play in a fenced yard, and do not let pets wander unsupervised. Report all animal bites to your city/town’s animal control officer. Securely cover all garbage cans so wild animals cannot scavenge for food. The Health Department posts its rabies data here . Windsor, NSW Print Edition What's On HOME LATEST NEWS BUSINESS SPORT COMMUNITY PROPERTY LIFE Directory Notice Board +Health Call WIRES, don’t handle bats Health warning after rise in bites and scratches and Hawkesbury has local colonies. , and Editorial Collective October 31, 2026 . 9:37 AM 2 min read X Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Share via Email Photo by Nils Bouillard / Unsplash Hawkesbury residents are being urged to call wildlife rescuers rather than handle injured or distressed bats, following a sharp increase in people requiring medical assessment after bites and scratches. The warning has local relevance, with a flying-fox colony near the intersection of Hawkesbury Valley Way and Macquarie Street in Windsor. ABC News has reported concerns about increased encounters between people and struggling flying-foxes during a suspected food shortage along the NSW coast. NSW Health says 43 people were assessed following bat bites or scratches between September 28 and October 10, compared with 10 during the same fortnight last year. Those figures represent people assessed after contact with bats, not confirmed infections or necessarily hospital admissions. The concern is Australian bat lyssavirus, a virus closely related to rabies that can be carried by fruit bats, also known as flying-foxes, and insect-eating microbats. Human infection is extremely rare, but there is no effective treatment once symptoms develop. NSW Health’s Director in Health Protection, Keira Glasgow, urged people to leave rescues to trained handlers. “If you see a bat that is injured or in distress, call your local wildlife rescue service and do not touch it,” she said. Food shortages can cause flying-foxes to remain in backyard feeding trees during daylight instead of returning to their usual colonies. A bat seen during the day is not necessarily infected, and its appearance cannot reliably indicate whether it carries the virus. Residents who find a bat injured, grounded or caught in netting should keep children and pets away and call WIRES on 1300 094 737. They should not attempt to pick it up, untangle it or manage the rescue themselves. Anyone bitten or scratched should immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, apply an antiviral antiseptic such as povidone-iodine, and seek urgent medical attention. This advice applies even to people previously vaccinated against rabies. Do not wait for symptoms. Simply living near a flying-fox colony or walking past roosting bats does not constitute a lyssavirus exposure. The warning concerns direct contact, particularly bites, scratches or saliva entering broken skin, the eyes, nose or mouth. Flying-foxes play an important role in pollination and seed dispersal. Calling trained rescuers helps protect both residents and wildlife. records.content: Health & Fitness Rabid Raccoon Found In Old Bridge Backyard An Old Bridge resident discovered a lethargic raccoon in their backyard Sunday: OLD BRIDGE, NJ — A "lethargic" raccoon found Sunday in the backyard of an Old Bridge home died, and later tested positive for the rabies virus, announced Middlesex County. On Sunday, Oct. 25, an Old Bridge resident discovered a lethargic raccoon in their backyard, in the vicinity of West Greystone Road and Old Bridge-Englishtown Road. Animal control responded and retrieved the raccoon. The raccoon was taken to the New Jersey Department of Health Laboratory for testing. It was reported on Wednesday, October 28 that it tested positive for rabies. Find out what's happening in Matawan-Aberdeenfor free with the latest updates from Patch. There were no human exposures and no animal exposures to the raccoon. This is the fifth rabid animal reported in Middlesex County for 2026 and the first rabid animal in Old Bridge. Find out what's happening in Matawan-Aberdeenfor free with the latest updates from Patch. Residents should report wild animals showing signs of unusual behavior to their local police department. Avoid contact with wild animals and immediately report any bites from wild or domestic animals to your local health department and consult a physician as soon as possible. Keep dogs on leashes at all times and make sure they are up to date on their rabies vaccinations. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for free Patch newsletters and alerts
